hints: Start by reminding yourself what makes any amine basic at the particle level, think about what the nitrogen lone pair must do to a proton.
Compare the nitrogen lone pair in $\text{RNH}_2$ with that in $\text{RCONH}_2$, consider where else the lone pair can interact when a $\text{C=O}$ group is directly attached.
walkthrough:
Picture what basic behaviour really means**
Think of basicity as a competition for a proton. An amine like $\text{RNH}_2$ has a lone pair localised on nitrogen that can readily form a dative bond to $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{RNH}_3^{+}$. The more available that lone pair is, the stronger the base.

See what the carbonyl does to the lone pair**
In an amide, $\text{R-C(=O)-NH}_2$, the nitrogen is directly joined to a carbonyl carbon. The nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the $\pi$ system of the $\text{C=O}$. You can draw it delocalised as $\text{R-C(O}^{-}\text{)=N}^{+}\text{H}_2$. Because the lone pair is pulled away from nitrogen and spread over the amide group, it is far less available to coordinate to $\text{H}^{+}$, so amides are much weaker bases, essentially neutral.

Final answer: Bases accept a proton / $\text{H}^{+}$ using a lone pair on N.
In amides the N lone pair is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group, so it is much less available to accept a proton than in amines.

hints: Count carbons in 2-phenylethylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, and work backwards from each reagent to see what functional group must have been present.
Recall which functional group is reduced by $\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}$ to a primary amine, and which functional group reacts with excess $\text{NH}_3$ to give a primary amine.
walkthrough:
Fix the carbon skeleton**
Look at the product, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. It has a phenyl ring plus a two carbon side chain ending in $\text{NH}_2$. Both M and N must already contain that $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ skeleton, only the terminal group is different.

Decode M from $\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}$**
Catalytic hydrogenation with $\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}$ converts a nitrile, $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$, into a primary amine, $\text{R-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. To get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, M must be one carbon shorter as the nitrile: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, written $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$.

Decode N from $\text{NH}_3$**
Excess ammonia converts a halogenoalkane into a primary amine by nucleophilic substitution: $\text{R-Br} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{R-NH}_2 + \text{NH}_4\text{Br}$. So N must be the same carbon skeleton with Br in place of $\text{NH}_2$: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.

Final answer: M is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ (phenylacetonitrile).
N is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ (2-bromoethylbenzene, any halogen acceptable as bromo/chloro/iodo analogue).

hints: Identify the change in reaction 1, an amide $\text{RCONH}_2$ becomes a primary amine $\text{RCH}_2\text{NH}_2$, decide what type of reagent removes the carbonyl oxygen.
walkthrough:
Recognise amide to amine reduction**
Reaction 1 converts $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2$, oxygen is removed as water on work up. This is reduction of an amide, and the classic reagent that is powerful enough is $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ (lithium aluminium hydride, dry ether, followed by acid hydrolysis).

hints: Look carefully at the left hand end of H, $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)CH}_2$, and at the nitrogen which is bonded to two carbons plus one hydrogen, count how many carbons are attached to N.
walkthrough:
Sort the three groups in H**
On the left you see $\text{CH}_3\text{-C(=O)-CH}_2$, a $\text{C=O}$ with two alkyl groups attached, that is a ketone. In the middle the nitrogen is bonded to two carbon groups ($\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2$ of the ring alkene) and one H, formula $\text{R}_2\text{NH}$. Two organic groups on N means a secondary, $2^{\circ}$, amine. The right hand ring contains the stated $\text{C=C}$ alkene.

Final answer: other functional group: ketone (carbonyl).
classification of amine: secondary / $2^{\circ}$ amine.

hints: Remember curly arrows always flow from an electron rich site to an electron poor site, locate the lone pair on ozone and the $\pi$ electrons of the alkene.

Think of the $\text{C=C}$ $\pi$ bond attacking the positively charged oxygen of $\text{O}_3$ while the $\text{O=O}$ $\pi$ bond shifts, forming two new $\text{C-O}$ bonds to close the five membered ozonide ring.
walkthrough:
Start the arrow from the nucleophile**
The ozone is drawn as $^{-}\text{O}-\text{O}^{+}\text{=O}$ with a lone pair on the negative oxygen. That lone pair is electron rich and the alkene carbon is the target, so draw the first curly arrow starting at the $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair and pointing to one carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond. This begins the first new $\text{C-O}$ bond.

Move the $\pi$ electrons to close the ring**
At the same time the $\text{C=C}$ $\pi$ pair swings to form the second $\text{C-O}$ bond to the terminal $\text{O}$ of the $\text{O=O}$ unit. To avoid exceeding the octet on oxygen, the $\text{O=O}$ $\pi$ bond must shift onto the central $\text{O}^{+}$, neutralising it. That gives the second arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to the right hand O, and the third arrow from the $\text{O=O}$ bond to $\text{O}^{+}$, completing the cyclic ozonide.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to C of $\text{C=C}$.
Curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ bond to the right hand O of $\text{O=O}$ and curly arrow from $\text{O=O}$ bond to $\text{O}^{+}$.

hints: Use Fig. 9.3 in reverse, ozonolysis splits $\text{C=C}$ into two $\text{C=O}$ groups, so to find K join the two carbonyl carbons of L back together with a double bond.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the dicarbonyl**
L is $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, octane-2,6-dione. In ozonolysis each $\text{C=O}$ carbon in the product was one end of the original $\text{C=C}$. Joining those two carbonyl carbons with a $\text{C=C}$ bond while keeping the rest of the chain gives a ring. Count: $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{14}$ fits a five membered ring with one double bond plus methyl and ethyl substituents. That is 1-methyl-2-ethylcyclopent-1-ene, whose cleavage opens the ring to exactly L.
Final answer: K is 1-methyl-2-ethylcyclopent-1-ene (five membered ring with $\text{C=C}$ bearing $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
